ANALYSIS

[10] I am of the opinion that the RPD erred in its analysis of the prospective risk for the appellants in the event that they return to Haiti and that they have established a profile suggesting that they would face a serious possibility of gender-related persecution based on their membership in the particular social group of single women without family protection, in light of the documentary evidence.

[11] The associate appellant is basing her claim entirely on the same facts as the principal appellant, and this analysis also applies to her.

[12] In reviewing this claim, I considered Guideline 4, which emphasizes the importance of considering the social, cultural, religious and economic context in which claimants find themselves.7
i. The Refugee Protection Division erred in its analysis of prospective risk

[13] The documentary evidence describes the scourge that is gender-based violence for women in Haiti.8 It indicates that violence against women is "widespread" and "chronic" in Haiti, being part of a culture of discrimination, which has an impact on their access to education and the labour market. Women therefore find themselves in a state of economic dependence and vulnerability with respect to men. This evidence also indicates that sexual assaults against women are common in Haiti and go unpunished. Such violence increased all the more because of the insecurity in camps for people displaced by the 2010 earthquake. According to the same evidence, the risk of violence increases considerably for women living in precarious conditions or in areas where criminality is omnipresent.9 The case law has also consistently recognized that in this context, support and protection for women come primarily from the family, the community and the diaspora.10

[14] In the present case, the RPD concluded that, in view of the level of education and financial situation of the principal appellant, who owns a house, the appellants did not exhibit the profile of women who are particularly vulnerable to the risk of gender-based violence in Haiti.11

[15] The appellants argue that the RPD failed to sufficiently consider all their particular circumstances in drawing this conclusion. I agree.

[17] In Josile,12 the Federal Court elaborated upon the factors to consider as part of a thorough analysis of the risk for Haitian women citing a fear of gender-related persecution. [18] It is thereby established that the evidence provided must demonstrate that there is a risk whose occurrence is "more than a mere possibility."14

[34] The appellants also refer to the documentary evidence34 indicating that the associate appellant's young age would make her [translation] "a preferred target for criminal gangs" and that the observation that she can resume attending university is not relevant to the assessment of her risk profile.35 I agree and consider that the documentary evidence weighs heavily in favour of the appellants since they have established that they have no male or family protection and that they live in an area where the risk of violence, including sexual violence, is high.

[35] In light of the foregoing, I consider that the appellants' allegation that they would be particularly vulnerable to the risk of persecution in Haiti as single women without family protection is corroborated in the objective evidence and that the RPD erred in its analysis.
ii. Determination of remedies

[36] Having concluded that the RPD erred in its analysis of the appellants' future, I must now examine how to remedy this.
a) Serious possibility of persecution is established

[37] Based on the objective evidence and the appellants' particular circumstances, I concluded that they would face a serious possibility of persecution in Haiti by reason of their membership in the particular social group of single women without family protection.

[38] Based on the documentary evidence, they would be particularly vulnerable to gender-based violence, including sexual violence.36 This type of violence is gender-based37 and may be characterized as severe abuses amounting to persecution under international law.38
b) State protection is inadequate

[39] The objective documentary evidence demonstrates in a clear and convincing manner that there is not adequate protection in Haiti for women who are victims of gender-based violence.

[40] In the broader context of ineffective judicial structures and a police force with limited awareness of the issue of violence against women, female victims face mistreatment by the police and the courts.39 Authorities frequently do not take these women seriously, do not accept their complaints or fail to consider critical evidence with a view to responding adequately to reports of gender-based violence.40

[41] In light of the discriminatory habits and practices deeply rooted in the concept of the inferiority of women within Haiti's judicial system,41 as well as a lack of resources to address crimes of this nature,42 it is established that the appellants would not have access to adequate state protection in Haiti.
c) There is no internal flight alternative

[42] In addition, given the current conditions of insecurity in Haiti,43 particularly for women without protection,44 the absence of family support and lack of adequate state protection exist everywhere in the country. As a result, the appellants have no internal flight alternative (IFA) anywhere else in Haiti.

[43] The documentary evidence indicates that violence against women is systemic and generalized and that the lack of adequate state protection extends everywhere in the country.45 46 I conclude that the fear of being raped or subjected to other forms of gender-based violence extends to the entire country of Haiti and that, consequently, there is no IFA.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] The principal appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a XXXX-year-old woman of Haitian nationality. The associate appellant, who is her XXXX-year-old daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, is also of Haitian nationality. They are from the Carrefour-Feuilles district located in the suburbs of Port-au-Prince.1

[2] In the event that they return to Haiti, they state that they fear being assaulted or killed by the principal appellant's ex-husband, who is the associate appellant's father. They also allege that they would face a risk of gender-based violence as single women without family protection.
* Conclusions of the Refugee Protection Division:

[3] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found the allegations of domestic violence and rape not credible in light of certain omissions and contradictions identified in the principal appellant's testimony, particularly concerning the date and circumstances of her divorce. It does not give any weight to the corroborating evidence presented in support of her testimony.

[4] Additionally, the RPD considered that the appellants did not exhibit the profile of women who are particularly vulnerable to the risk of gender-based violence in Haiti, given the principal appellant's level of education and financial situation. For these reasons, the RPD concluded that there was a lack of prospective risk.2
* Grounds of appeal:

[5] Primarily, the RPD's conclusions in relation to the appellants' prospective risk as women who are vulnerable to the risk of gender-based violence in Haiti are being disputed.3 Their arguments are summarized as follows:
a. The RPD based its conclusions on speculation;
b. The RPD failed to consider the evidence before it concerning gender-based violence in Haiti in coming to an erroneous conclusion concerning the risk faced by the appellants; and
c. The RPD erred in failing to consider Chairperson's Guideline 4 concerning Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution4 (Guideline 4) in a significant or sensitive manner as it was required to.
* Determinative issue:

[6] The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is the prospective risk.
DETERMINATION

[7] For the reasons set out below, I consider that the RPD erred in its conclusions regarding the lack of prospective risk, which is determinative in view of the appellants' profile as single women without family protection.

[8] The appeal is allowed. I substitute the determination of the RPD with my own determination that the appellants are Convention refugees.5
ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[9] The standard of review in this appeal is the standard of correctness.6 I conducted an independent review of the evidence, including the recording of the RPD hearing and the appellants' record. The appellants did not present any new evidence in support of their appeal, nor did they request an oral hearing before the RAD.
ANALYSIS

[10] I am of the opinion that the RPD erred in its analysis of the prospective risk for the appellants in the event that they return to Haiti and that they have established a profile suggesting that they would face a serious possibility of gender-related persecution based on their membership in the particular social group of single women without family protection, in light of the documentary evidence.
[11] The associate appellant is basing her claim entirely on the same facts as the principal appellant, and this analysis also applies to her.

[12] In reviewing this claim, I considered Guideline 4, which emphasizes the importance of considering the social, cultural, religious and economic context in which claimants find themselves.7
i. The Refugee Protection Division erred in its analysis of prospective risk

[13] The documentary evidence describes the scourge that is gender-based violence for women in Haiti.8 It indicates that violence against women is "widespread" and "chronic" in Haiti, being part of a culture of discrimination, which has an impact on their access to education and the labour market. Women therefore find themselves in a state of economic dependence and vulnerability with respect to men. This evidence also indicates that sexual assaults against women are common in Haiti and go unpunished. Such violence increased all the more because of the insecurity in camps for people displaced by the 2010 earthquake. According to the same evidence, the risk of violence increases considerably for women living in precarious conditions or in areas where criminality is omnipresent.9 The case law has also consistently recognized that in this context, support and protection for women come primarily from the family, the community and the diaspora.10

[14] In the present case, the RPD concluded that, in view of the level of education and financial situation of the principal appellant, who owns a house, the appellants did not exhibit the profile of women who are particularly vulnerable to the risk of gender-based violence in Haiti.11
[15] The appellants argue that the RPD failed to sufficiently consider all their particular circumstances in drawing this conclusion. I agree.

[16] Following my independent review of all the evidence on the record and, above all, the appellants' particular situation, I am of the opinion that the RPD's approach in this respect was not sufficiently thorough and that it failed to consider all the relevant information in determining their degree of vulnerability.

[17] In Josile,12 the Federal Court elaborated upon the factors to consider as part of a thorough analysis of the risk for Haitian women citing a fear of gender-related persecution. These factors include place of residence, the family context, the issue of adequate state protection in the absence of male protection and the particular circumstances.13
[18] It is thereby established that the evidence provided must demonstrate that there is a risk whose occurrence is "more than a mere possibility."14
[19] In the present case, the principal appellant is a divorced woman without a male presence in her family, and the associate appellant is a single, XXXX-year-old woman who lives with her.

[20] Based on the principal appellant's testimony, only her aunt, who has psychological problems, is currently living in the house, and she has no other close relatives.15 Before she left, she was living there alone with her daughter after her mother's death in 2016.16

[21] The appellants argue that the male presence in the family is frequently held in the case law to be able to provide a certain form of protection.17 In its absence, the appellants consequently find themselves in a situation of greater vulnerability to the sexual violence that, according to the documentary evidence, affects mainly women who are separated and living in urban areas.18

[22] In their memorandum, the appellants state in this regard that their house in Carrefour-Feuilles is located in a disadvantaged area where insecurity prevails, thereby contributing to their risk, and that this factor was not considered by the RPD.

[23] They confirmed at the hearing that their house is located in the disadvantaged district of Carrefour-Feuilles, at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, where the principal appellant had lived since age XXXX.19 This address is also corroborated by various evidence on the record.20

[24] This is also confirmed by the documentary evidence, which indicates that throughout the events of February 2019, Carrefour-Feuilles was the backdrop of shootouts between rival gangs that led many families to abandon their homes and take refuge in churches or with family or friends living in other communities.21 This district is identified as one of those where criminal gangs are active,22 including the group formerly controlled by Sony Jean, also known as Ti Je.23

[25] The appellants had no other housing and testified that they had been temporarily displaced following the 2010 earthquake. They had nowhere else to go and slept in the street, in tents and then at a school across from their damaged home.24

[26] The appellants argue further that the documentary evidence confirms that sexual violence is used as a weapon of war, among other things, by armed gangs which are rampant in the slums of Port-au-Prince and "disadvantaged metropolitan areas."25

[27] According to the documentary evidence, promiscuity is often the same in these areas as in camps for displaced persons, and it is difficult to complain to the police without fear of retaliation in these districts controlled by gangs. The rapists are frequently neighbours, husbands or community members. The victims hesitate even to report rape to any doctors they consult following the assault. [Translation] "...[F]or many women, their only hope for survival is to find a 'protector,' a husband or a boyfriend who is a gang member and therefore more respected. Or to start a new life by joining the ranks of the diaspora."26

[28] In my opinion, this situation is particularly relevant in light of the [translation] "gang war" currently raging in the Port-au-Prince area.27 It has been reported that among the people displaced by the violence, many are victims [translation] "of sexual abuse, including rape...in host families," with some persons forced to make the "offer of 'sex for shelter'."28

[29] Considering that the appellants' house is located in an area where this "gang war" is currently raging and that they testified previously that they had nowhere else to stay, there is also a serious possibility that they will find themselves in a situation where they are displaced by violence and face a higher risk of sexual abuse in the event that they return.

[30] Lastly, the appellants argue that the principal appellant's work as a civil engineer requires her to travel to other regions for extended periods for field feasibility studies, that there are not many women in her industry,29 which exposes her to additional risks, and that her daughter is then left alone.30

[31] I agree with the appellants that in view of the evidence on the record, which reports serious employment-related discrimination against women,31 32 the principal appellant would, on a balance of probabilities, have no other option but to continue this type of work in order to provide for their needs. This situation creates additional vulnerability for them both.

[32] The RPD had concluded in this respect that the principal appellant could hire a domestic worker to offset her absence as she had done in the past and that she was [translation] "an independent woman accustomed to living in a man's world in which she has had to struggle."33

[33] I disagree with this conclusion, since I consider that being an independent woman accustomed to living in a man's world does not correspond to an effective form of protection and has no impact on the objective situation of the appellants, who find themselves without family protection in a region where criminality and armed gangs are omnipresent and that this would not be offset merely by the possibility of hiring a domestic worker.

[34] The appellants also refer to the documentary evidence34 indicating that the associate appellant's young age would make her [translation] "a preferred target for criminal gangs" and that the observation that she can resume attending university is not relevant to the assessment of her risk profile.35 I agree and consider that the documentary evidence weighs heavily in favour of the appellants since they have established that they have no male or family protection and that they live in an area where the risk of violence, including sexual violence, is high.

[35] In light of the foregoing, I consider that the appellants' allegation that they would be particularly vulnerable to the risk of persecution in Haiti as single women without family protection is corroborated in the objective evidence and that the RPD erred in its analysis.
ii. Determination of remedies

[36] Having concluded that the RPD erred in its analysis of the appellants' future, I must now examine how to remedy this.
a) Serious possibility of persecution is established

[37] Based on the objective evidence and the appellants' particular circumstances, I concluded that they would face a serious possibility of persecution in Haiti by reason of their membership in the particular social group of single women without family protection.

[38] Based on the documentary evidence, they would be particularly vulnerable to gender-based violence, including sexual violence.36 This type of violence is gender-based37 and may be characterized as severe abuses amounting to persecution under international law.38
b) State protection is inadequate
[39] The objective documentary evidence demonstrates in a clear and convincing manner that there is not adequate protection in Haiti for women who are victims of gender-based violence.

[40] In the broader context of ineffective judicial structures and a police force with limited awareness of the issue of violence against women, female victims face mistreatment by the police and the courts.39 Authorities frequently do not take these women seriously, do not accept their complaints or fail to consider critical evidence with a view to responding adequately to reports of gender-based violence.40

[41] In light of the discriminatory habits and practices deeply rooted in the concept of the inferiority of women within Haiti's judicial system,41 as well as a lack of resources to address crimes of this nature,42 it is established that the appellants would not have access to adequate state protection in Haiti.
c) There is no internal flight alternative

[42] In addition, given the current conditions of insecurity in Haiti,43 particularly for women without protection,44 the absence of family support and lack of adequate state protection exist everywhere in the country. As a result, the appellants have no internal flight alternative (IFA) anywhere else in Haiti.

[43] The documentary evidence indicates that violence against women is systemic and generalized and that the lack of adequate state protection extends everywhere in the country.45 46 I conclude that the fear of being raped or subjected to other forms of gender-based violence extends to the entire country of Haiti and that, consequently, there is no IFA.
CONCLUSION

[44] For all these reasons, I determine that the RPD erred in concluding that the appellants would not face a serious possibility of persecution by reason of their particular vulnerability to gender-based violence as single women without family protection if they returned to Haiti.

[45] The appeal is allowed. I set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute it with my own determination that the appellants are Convention refugees.
